A formula called the Pythagorean Theorem shows the relationship between the sides of a right triangle.
The Pythagorean Theorem states that the square of the length of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the lengths of the legs.

The lengths of the sides of a right triangle are used to form the six trigonometric functions.
DISCUSSION
FUNCTIONS - A function is like a machine that takes a specific input and assigns a specific output.
Since the y values depend upon the x values we say that y is a function of x and can replace the y with f(x).
Two different inputs can result in the same output, but the same input cannot result in different outputs.
The sine of the other angle in the triangle is found using the same method.
These functions depend on the size of the angle, not the size of the triangle. Let's examine this further.
These two right triangles have the same size angles but the lengths of the sides are different.
Since the angles of the triangles are the same, the ratios of the corresponding sides are equal.
The ratios are dependent on the size of the angle and are considered functions of the angle.
These ratios form the six trigonometric functions.
The six trigonometric functions will be easier to remember using the relationship of the sides to the angle.
For example, the sine of an angle is the opposite side over the hypotenuse. Sine is usually abbreviated sin.

A circle with a radius of 1 unit is called the unit circle. The unit circle is used to further illustrate the six trigonometric functions.
An angle is placed on the graph with the vertex at the origin and the initial side along the X-axis. The angle is said to be in standard position.
A right triangle is formed when a line is drawn from the point P to the X-axis. The hypotenuse is the radius of the circle.
Since the side adjacent to the angle has a value of X and the opposite side has a value of Y, the trigonometric functions can be written using X and Y.
The radius of the circle is 1 so sine equals Y and cosine equals X. Now any point on the circle can be identified by the sine and cosine of the angle.
For example, cos p/6 equals S3/2 and sin p/6 equals 1/2 so the coordinates of the point on the circle are (S3/2, 1/2)..
The sine and cosine of equivalent angles in other quadrants become negative as the X or Y value becomes negative.
Once the sine and cosine of an angle are known, the values for other trigonometric functions can be found.
TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS - Remember the six trigonometric functions.
The cosecant is the reciprocal of the sine value and the secant is the reciprocal of the cosine value.
The tangent is found by placing the sine value over the cosine value and the cotangent is the cosine value over the sine value.
